html:
A Buddhist temple on the slopes of Mount Otowa, in the eastern hills of Kyoto, given to the worship of Kannon, the bodhisattva of mercy (Avalokiteshvara). Its name means "pure water", after the Otowa waterfall on its grounds. Its founding is known only from legend: in 778 a monk of Kōfuku-ji in Nara followed a dream to the falls, and in 780 the general Sakanoue no Tamuramaro is said to have given his own house as the main hall. That makes it one of the few temples in Kyoto older than the capital itself, founded in 794.

The main hall stands on a steep slope, and its wide wooden stage juts out over the hillside on tall pillars, built without a single nail. In the Edo period people leapt the 13 m from the stage in the belief that a wish would be granted if they lived; 234 jumps were recorded before the practice was banned in 1872, and "to jump off the stage at Kiyomizu" still means to take the plunge. Below the hall, three streams of the waterfall fall into a pond, and visitors drink from them. The grounds also hold a three-storey pagoda and the Jishu Shrine to a god of love and good matches.

By the mid-Heian period it was a well-known Kannon temple, mentioned in The Tale of Genji. It long belonged to the Hossō sect of Kōfuku-ji, which drew it into that temple's quarrels with Enryaku-ji: warrior monks from Enryaku-ji burned it in 1165, and it burned again in 1469 in the Ōnin War, one of nine recorded fires between 1063 and 1629. The present main hall was rebuilt in 1633 with a gift from the shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu. It is part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
